[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +#!/usr/bin/env bash
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +# Print Unix time in milliseconds without relying on date's non-portable %3N
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +# width handling. Some implementations emit all nine nanosecond digits for
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +# %3N, which turns a millisecond deadline into a nanosecond-scale value.
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +epoch_millis() {
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +  local timestamp seconds nanoseconds milliseconds extra
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +  timestamp="$(date '+%s %N')" || return 1
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +  read -r seconds nanoseconds extra <<<"$timestamp"
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +  [[ "$seconds" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && -z "${extra:-}" ]] || return 1
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +  if [[ "$nanoseconds" =~ ^[0-9]{3,9}$ ]]; then
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +    milliseconds="${nanoseconds:0:3}"
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +  else
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +    # BSD date prints a literal %N. Second precision is conservative and keeps
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +    # deadlines and freshness receipts in the documented millisecond unit.
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +    milliseconds=000
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +  fi
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +  printf '%s%s\n' "$seconds" "$milliseconds"
[2026-09-23T20:11:48.178Z] [STDERR] +}

[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +# Print Unix time in milliseconds without relying on date's non-portable %3N
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +# width handling. Some implementations emit all nine nanosecond digits for
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +# %3N, which turns a millisecond deadline into a nanosecond-scale value.
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +epoch_millis() {
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +  local timestamp seconds nanoseconds milliseconds extra
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +  timestamp="$(date '+%s %N')" || return 1
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +  read -r seconds nanoseconds extra <<<"$timestamp"
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +  [[ "$seconds" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && -z "${extra:-}" ]] || return 1
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +  if [[ "$nanoseconds" =~ ^[0-9]{3,9}$ ]]; then
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +    milliseconds="${nanoseconds:0:3}"
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +  else
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +    # BSD date prints a literal %N. Second precision is conservative and keeps
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +    # deadlines and freshness receipts in the documented millisecond unit.
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +    milliseconds=000
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +  fi
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +  printf '%s%s\n' "$seconds" "$milliseconds"
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.872Z] [STDERR] +}

[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +# Print Unix time in milliseconds without relying on date's non-portable %3N
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +# width handling. Some implementations emit all nine nanosecond digits for
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +# %3N, which turns a millisecond deadline into a nanosecond-scale value.
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +epoch_millis() {
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +  local timestamp seconds nanoseconds milliseconds extra
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +  timestamp="$(date '+%s %N')" || return 1
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +  read -r seconds nanoseconds extra <<<"$timestamp"
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +  [[ "$seconds" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && -z "${extra:-}" ]] || return 1
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +  if [[ "$nanoseconds" =~ ^[0-9]{3,9}$ ]]; then
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +    milliseconds="${nanoseconds:0:3}"
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +  else
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +    # BSD date prints a literal %N. Second precision is conservative and keeps
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +    # deadlines and freshness receipts in the documented millisecond unit.
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +    milliseconds=000
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +  fi
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +  printf '%s%s\n' "$seconds" "$milliseconds"
[2026-09-23T22:17:27.944Z] [STDERR] +}

[2026-09-23T22:31:17.518Z] [STDOUT] ## Summary

- add a portable epoch-millisecond helper for launcher and independently deployed OPS scripts
- use the helper for gateway deadlines, elapsed latency, completion receipts, readiness polling, and canary cache busters
- reject nanosecond-scale future completion receipts and bound public latency to a sane 60-second schema window
- install the helper beside the health probe and gateway escrow reconciler without adding dependencies to unrelated minimal launchers

## Root cause and reproduction

The public gateway health producer was using `date +%s%3N`. On the deployed date implementation, `%3N` emits all nine fractional digits, so a 16 ms interval is published as 16,000,000 ms and request deadlines use the wrong unit. The live health document exposed multi-million `latency_ms` values while readiness remained unavailable.

`test-epoch-millis.sh` reproduces the unit expansion, verifies a 16 ms result after conversion, covers implementations without `%N`, and prevents operational scripts from reintroducing the non-portable expression. The readiness test also rejects a nanosecond-scale completion timestamp before accepting a fresh, causally ordered receipt.

## Verification

- `make shellcheck` (full repository, ShellCheck v0.11.0)
- portable epoch-millisecond regression
- gateway health and public traffic-readiness tests
- gateway escrow and inference retry tests
- profiles, continuity, domain CLI, command-result, and minimal-launcher fixtures
- all remaining `make test` recipes before and after the JOIN preflight fixture

Local environment note: `test-join-preflight-diagnostics.sh` is wall-clock sensitive here. Its five-second recovery window permits only two of the three expected observations. The unchanged test fails the same way on upstream `main`; surrounding recipes pass on this branch.

## Deployment status

Read-only public verification shows the new health schema is already served, but DevNet still reports Gonka v0.2.15 / DAPI v0.2.15-post3 and the gateway is not runtime-routable. This checkout does not contain the owner-held `$HOME/.gdc-data/.env`, so this PR does not perform the stateful DevShard v5 / Gonka v0.2.16 rollout. Owner-authorized `gdc ops site`, `gdc ops edge`, and live canary acceptance remain required.
